units.text: INT. SISTERS - CONTINUOUS
You can come to-morrow and fetch these documents.... Go along....
units.name: ANDREY

units.text: Pause.
He’s gone.
units.name: ANDREY

units.text: A ring.
Yes, yes....
units.name: ANDREY

units.text: Stretches himself and slowly goes into his own room.
Behind the scene the nurse is singing a lullaby to the child.
MASHA and VERSHININ come in.
While they talk, a maidservant lights candles and a lamp.
I don’t know.
units.name: MASHA

units.text: Pause.

I don’t know. Of course, habit counts for a great deal. After father’s death, for instance, it took us a long time to get used to the absence of orderlies. But, apart from habit, it seems to me in all fairness that, however it may be in other towns, the best and most-educated people are army men.
units.name: MASHA

units.text: I’m thirsty. I should like some tea.
units.name: VERSHININ

units.text: Glancing at her watch.

They’ll bring some soon. I was given in marriage when I was eighteen, and I was afraid of my husband because he was a teacher and I’d only just left school. He then seemed to me frightfully wise and learned and important. And now, unfortunately, that has changed.
units.name: MASHA

units.text: Yes... yes.
units.name: VERSHININ

units.text: I don’t speak of my husband, I’ve grown used to him, but civilians in general are so often coarse, impolite, uneducated. Their rudeness offends me, it angers me. I suffer when I see that a man isn’t quite sufficiently refined, or delicate, or polite. I simply suffer agonies when I happen to be among schoolmasters, my husband’s colleagues.
units.name: MASHA

units.text: Yes.... It seems to me that civilians and army men are equally interesting, in this town, at any rate. It’s all the same! If you listen to a member of the local intelligentsia, whether to civilian or military, he will tell you that he’s sick of his wife, sick of his house, sick of his estate, sick of his horses.... We Russians are extremely gifted in the direction of thinking on an exalted plane, but, tell me, why do we aim so low in real life? Why?
units.name: VERSHININ

units.text: Why?
units.name: MASHA

units.text: Why is a Russian sick of his children, sick of his wife? And why are his wife and children sick of him?
units.name: VERSHININ

units.text: You’re a little downhearted to-day.
units.name: MASHA

units.text: Perhaps I am. I haven’t had any dinner, I’ve had nothing since the morning. My daughter is a little unwell, and when my girls are ill, I get very anxious and my conscience tortures me because they have such a mother. Oh, if you had seen her to-day! What a trivial personality! We began quarrelling at seven in the morning and at nine I slammed the door and went out.
units.name: VERSHININ

units.text: Pause.
I never speak of her, it’s strange that I bear my complaints to you alone.
units.name: VERSHININ

units.text: Kisses her hand.
Don’t be angry with me. I haven’t anybody but you, nobody at all....
units.name: VERSHININ

units.text: Pause.
What a noise in the oven. Just before father’s death there was a noise in the pipe, just like that.
units.name: MASHA

units.text: Are you superstitious?
units.name: VERSHININ

units.text: Yes.
units.name: MASHA

units.text: That’s strange.
units.name: VERSHININ

units.text: Kisses her hand.
You are a splendid, wonderful woman. Splendid, wonderful! It is dark here, but I see your sparkling eyes.
units.name: VERSHININ

units.text: Sits on another chair.
There is more light here.
units.name: MASHA

units.text: I love you, love you, love you... I love your eyes, your movements, I dream of them.... Splendid, wonderful woman!
units.name: VERSHININ

units.text: Laughing.
When you talk to me like that, I laugh; I don’t know why, for I’m afraid. Don’t repeat it, please....
units.name: MASHA

units.text: In an undertone.
No, go on, it’s all the same to me....
units.name: MASHA

units.text: Covers her face with her hands.
Somebody’s coming, let’s talk about something else.
units.name: MASHA

units.text: IRINA and TUZENBACH come in through the dining-room.

My surname is really triple. I am called Baron Tuzenbach-Krone-Altschauer, but I am Russian and Orthodox, the same as you. There is very little German left in me, unless perhaps it is the patience and the obstinacy with which I bore you. I see you home every night.
units.name: TUZENBACH

units.text: How tired I am!
units.name: IRINA

units.text: And I’ll come to the telegraph office to see you home every day for ten or twenty years, until you drive me away.
units.name: TUZENBACH

units.text: He sees MASHA and VERSHININ; joyfully.
